claim: Follicle elongation is normal in fat2 mutants during stages 3-7 with an aspect ratio of 1.6.
source: Follicle elongation is normal in fat2 mutants during the first stages (3–7) with an AR of 1.6 (Figure 1a–d).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1d and direct observation in Figure 1c.

claim: At least two mechanistically distinct elongation phases control follicle elongation: a first phase (stages 3-7) independent of fat2, rotation and ECM basal polarization, and a later phase (stages 8-14) requiring fat2.
source: Thus, at least two mechanistically distinct elongation phases control follicle elongation, a first phase (stages 3–7), which is independent of fat2, rotation and ECM basal polarization, and a later phase (stages 8–14), which requires fat2.
evidence: Based on kinetic analysis of fat2 mutants showing normal elongation until stage 7 but defects in later stages.

claim: The absence of an elongation defect of clonal loss-of-function of vkg before stages 7-8 is consistent with fat2-independent early elongation.
source: This observation is consistent with the absence of an elongation defect of clonal loss-of-function of vkg before stages 7–8 (Bilder and Haigo, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Bilder and Haigo, 2012.

claim: Pak mutant follicles never elongate.
source: To try to identify the mechanism that regulates the early phase of follicle elongation, we first analyzed trans-heterozygous Pak mutant follicles, which never elongate (Conder et al., 2007) (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by citation to Conder et al., 2007 and shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The Pak gene encodes a Pak family serine/threonine kinase that localizes at the FE basal domain.
source: The Pak gene encodes a Pak family serine/threonine kinase that localizes at the FE basal domain.
evidence: Statement about the molecular identity and localization of Pak protein.

claim: Pak mutants show abnormalities including the presence of more than one germline cyst and abnormal interfollicular filaments.
source: Pak mutants also show many other abnormalities, such as the presence of more than one germline cyst and abnormal interfollicular filaments ([Vlachos et al., 2015] and not shown).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vlachos et al., 2015.

claim: In WT follicles, polar cells are localized at the follicle AP axis extremities.
source: In WT follicles, polar cells are localized at the follicle AP axis extremities (Figure 1b).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1b with FasIII staining marking polar cells.

claim: In Pak mutants, a single polar cell cluster or two clusters close to each other are observed.
source: Conversely, in Pak mutants, we observed a single polar cell cluster or two clusters close to each other (Figure 1e).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1e with FasIII staining.

claim: Pak is required for polar cell positioning.
source: This suggests that Pak is required for polar cell positioning, although a role in the specification or survival of these cells cannot be excluded, which in turn could play a role in defining the elongation axis.
evidence: Inferred from observation of polar cell mislocalization in Pak mutants.

claim: Removing one copy of Pvr in Pak mutants frequently but not always restores normal positioning of polar cells.
source: By using flies that are heterozygous for a Pvr allele and mutant for Pak, we observed that the normal positioning of polar cells is frequently but not always restored (Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Restoring polar cell position by removing one copy of Pvr in Pak mutants strongly rescues follicle elongation.
source: The statistical comparison of the elongation coefficients clearly shows that restoring polar cell position by removing one copy of Pvr in Pak mutants strongly rescues follicle elongation (Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Mosaic follicles containing FC clones that are mutant for myospheroid (mys) show a round follicle phenotype at early stages.
source: Although not been fully demonstrated in this context, Pak often works as part of the integrin signaling network, and mosaic follicles containing FC clones that are mutant for myospheroid (mys), which encodes the main fly β-integrin subunit, also show a round follicle phenotype at early stages (Haigo and Bilder, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haigo and Bilder, 2011.

claim: In some follicles containing mys mutant clones, polar cells are mispositioned.
source: We noticed that in some follicles containing mys mutant clones, polar cells are mispositioned, a defect generally observed when at least one polar cell is mutant.
evidence: Direct observation in mosaic follicles.

claim: The polar cell positioning defect is associated with the round follicle phenotype in mys mutants.
source: Importantly, the polar cell positioning defect is associated with the round follicle phenotype (Figure 1j, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1j and Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: In mosaic follicles in which polar cell positioning was not affected, the round egg phenotype is never observed at early stages, even with large mutant clones.
source: Conversely, in mosaic follicles in which polar cell positioning was not affected, the round egg phenotype is never observed at early stages, even with large mutant clones (Figure 1h and Figure 1—figure supplement 1f, Video 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1h and Figure 1—figure supplement 1f, Video 2.

claim: The elongation coefficient of mosaic follicles that have normal polar cell positioning is much higher than that for those with abnormal polar cells.
source: In agreement, the elongation coefficient of mosaic follicles that have normal polar cell positioning is much higher than that for those with abnormal polar cells (Figure 1j).
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1j.

claim: pak and mys mutants are not required for the early phase of elongation once polar cells are well-placed and thus affect this phase indirectly.
source: Thus, together, these results indicate that pak and mys mutants are not required for the early phase of elongation once polar cells are well-placed and thus affect this phase indirectly.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that elongation is normal when polar cells are correctly positioned in these mutants.

claim: Polar cells are required to define the follicle elongation axis.
source: The results also strongly suggest that polar cells are required to define the follicle elongation axis.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between polar cell positioning and elongation defects.

claim: Polar cells are important for the differentiation of the surrounding FCs once the follicle is formed.
source: Once the follicle is formed, polar cells are important for the differentiation of the surrounding FCs.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about polar cell function.

claim: From stage 9 of oogenesis, FCs change their morphology upon activation by Unpaired (Upd), a ligand for the JAK-STAT pathway, which is exclusively produced by polar cells throughout oogenesis.
source: From stage 9 of oogenesis, FCs change their morphology upon activation by Unpaired (Upd), a ligand for the JAK-STAT pathway, which is exclusively produced by polar cells throughout oogenesis (Silver and Montell, 2001; Xi et al., 2003; McGregor et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Silver and Montell, 2001; Xi et al., 2003; McGregor et al., 2002.

claim: During the early stages of oogenesis, the JAK-STAT pathway is active in all the main body FCs.
source: During the early stages of oogenesis, the pathway is active in all the main body FCs (Figure 2b).
evidence: Shown using 10xStatGFP reporter in Figure 2b.

claim: Differences in STAT activity between the poles and the mediolateral region start at about stage 3, concomitantly with the beginning of elongation.
source: Moreover, we observed differences in GFP expression level (and thus STAT activity) between the poles and the mediolateral region, starting at about stage 3, concomitantly with the beginning of elongation (Figure 2b,h).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2b,h using 10xStatGFP reporter.

claim: At stages 5-7, a gradient of STAT activity forms, with strong GFP expression at each pole and very weak or no signal in the large mediolateral part of each follicle.
source: At later stages (5–7), these expression differences lead to the formation of a gradient of STAT activity, as indicated by strong GFP expression at each pole and very weak or no signal in the large mediolateral part of each follicle (Figure 2b,h, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2b,h, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a using 10xStatGFP reporter.

claim: The spatiotemporal pattern of JAK-STAT activation is consistent with a potential role of this pathway in follicle elongation.
source: Thus, the spatiotemporal pattern of JAK-STAT activation is consistent with a potential role of this pathway in follicle elongation.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between JAK-STAT gradient formation and elongation timing.

claim: Upd knockdown using upd:GAL4 or tj:GAL4 results in follicles that are significantly rounder than control follicles during the early stages.
source: Upd knockdown was performed using either upd:GAL4 that is specifically expressed in the polar cells (Khammari et al., 2011) or tj:GAL4 that is expressed in all FCs, and then analyzed only in follicles that contained one germline cyst and correctly placed polar cells. During the early stages, with both drivers, such follicles are significantly rounder than control follicles (Figure 2a,c,g and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2a,c,g and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e, with citation to Khammari et al., 2011.

claim: JAK-STAT pathway has a role in early elongation.
source: This indicates a role for JAK-STAT pathway in early elongation and confirms the causal link between polar cells and early elongation.
evidence: Inferred from upd knockdown experiments showing elongation defects.

claim: Knockdown of Stat92E using Fru:GAL4 affects early elongation.
source: Moreover, knockdown of Stat92E using a driver that is specifically expressed at the poles (Fru:GAL4) also affects early elongation (Figure 2d,g and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e), suggesting a transcriptional control of elongation by JAK-STAT (Borensztejn et al., 2013).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2d,g and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e, with citation to Borensztejn et al., 2013.

claim: Both Upd secreted by the polar cells and JAK-STAT activation in FCs are required for follicle elongation.
source: These results are the first examples of loss of function with an effect only on early elongation and independent of polar cells position, and indicate that both Upd secreted by the polar cells and JAK-STAT activation in FCs arerequired for follicle elongation.
evidence: Based on upd and Stat92E knockdown experiments.

claim: Clonal ectopic upd overexpression completely blocks follicle elongation, without affecting polar cell positioning.
source: Moreover, clonal ectopic upd overexpression completely blocks follicle elongation, without affecting polar cell positioning (Figure 2e), demonstrating that Upd is not only a prerequisite for the elongation but the signal that defines its axis (n = 20).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2e with n=20 follicles analyzed.

claim: General expression of HopTum, a gain-of-function mutation of fly JAK, that disrupts the pattern of JAK-SAT activation also affects follicle elongation.
source: Similarly, general expression of HopTum, a gain-of-function mutation of fly JAK, that disrupts the pattern of JAK-SAT activation also affects follicle elongation (Figure 2f,g and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2f,g and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Spatial control of JAK-STAT pathway activation is required for follicle elongation.
source: Thus, spatial control of JAK-STAT pathway activation is required for follicle elongation.
evidence: Inferred from HopTum gain-of-function experiments disrupting JAK-STAT pattern.

claim: Upd secretion by polar cells and the subsequent gradient of JAK-STAT activation act as developmental cues that define the follicle elongation axis during the early stages of oogenesis.
source: Altogether, these results show that Upd secretion by polar cells and the subsequent gradient of JAK-STAT activation act as developmental cues that define the follicle elongation axis during the early stages of oogenesis.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple JAK-STAT manipulation experiments.

claim: The knockdown in all FCs of spaghetti squash (sqh), the MyoII regulatory subunit, leads to a significant decrease in the elongation coefficient and in follicle AR from stage 4.
source: The knockdown in all FCs of spaghetti squash (sqh), the MyoII regulatory subunit, leads to a significant decrease in the elongation coefficient and in follicle AR from stage 4 (Figure 3a–b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b,c), indicating that MyoII is the motor of early elongation.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3a–b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: MyoII is the motor of early elongation.
source: The knockdown in all FCs of spaghetti squash (sqh), the MyoII regulatory subunit, leads to a significant decrease in the elongation coefficient and in follicle AR from stage 4 (Figure 3a–b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b,c), indicating that MyoII is the motor of early elongation.
evidence: Inferred from sqh knockdown causing elongation defects.

claim: At early stages, MyoII is strongly enriched at the apical cortex.
source: Moreover, at these stages, MyoII is strongly enriched at the apical cortex, suggesting that its main activity is on this domain of the FCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and Figure 5c) (Wang and Riechmann, 2007).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and Figure 5c, with citation to Wang and Riechmann, 2007.

claim: The transient accumulation of MyoII is associated with a contraction of the apical domain, which is followed by a relaxation when the MyoII signal decreases.
source: Accordingly, using a GFP trap line for Bazooka (Baz-GFP), which concentrates at the zonula adherens and marks the periphery of the apical domain, we observed that the transient accumulation of MyoII is associated with a contraction of this domain, which is followed by a relaxation when the MyoII signal decreases (Figure 3c–e, Video 4).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3c–e and Video 4 using live imaging.

claim: The approximate duration of a pulse is about three minutes.
source: Although we did not find a clear period because cells can pause for a variable time between two contractions, the approximate duration of a pulse was about three minutes.
evidence: Based on live imaging observations.

claim: Cross-correlation analysis confirms the association between MyoII and pulses, and reveals that Sqh accumulation slightly precedes the reduction of the apical surface.
source: Cross-correlation analysis on many cells from several follicles (n = 86) confirms the association between MyoII and pulses, and reveals that Sqh accumulation slightly precedes the reduction of the apical surface, arguing that it is the motor responsible for these contractions (Figure 3f).
evidence: Quantitative cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 3f with n=86 cells.

claim: Inhibiting the activity of Rho kinase (rok) using Y-27632 reduces follicle cells' surface variation by ~30%.
source: Inhibiting the activity of Rho kinase (rok), the main regulator of MyoII, using Y-27632, reduces follicle cells' surface variation by ~30% (Figure 3g).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3g using pharmacological inhibition.

claim: MyoII drives apical pulsing during early stages.
source: Thus, MyoII drives apical pulsing during early stages.
evidence: Inferred from correlation analysis and Rok inhibition experiments.

claim: Basal pulses, which are important for the second phase of elongation, have been shown to be anisotropic from stage 9.
source: From stage 9, basal pulses, which are important for the second phase of elongation, have been shown to be anisotropic (He et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to He et al., 2010.

claim: Quantification of axis length variations showed that the apical pulses were isotropic, both in the mediolateral and polar regions.
source: However, quantification of axis length variations showed that the apical pulses were isotropic, both in the mediolateral and polar regions (Figure 3h).
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3h.

claim: There is no noticeable apical planar cell polarization of Myosin II and Baz.
source: Consistent with the isotropic nature of the pulses, we failed to detect any oriented enrichment of these proteins, indicating the absence of noticeable apical planar cell polarization of the motor that generates early elongation (Figure 3i,j).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3i,j through quantification of protein localization.

claim: MyoII induces apical pulses and early elongation.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that MyoII induces apical pulses and early elongation.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on MyoII knockdown and activity analysis.

claim: At stage 3, cells undergo contractions and relaxations asynchronously in the mediolateral region.
source: We therefore monitored the mediolateral region of stage 3 and 7 follicles. At stage 3, cells undergo contractions and relaxations asynchronously (Figure 4a, Video 5).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4a and Video 5 through live imaging.

claim: At stage 7, cells in the mediolateral region were much less active than at stage 3.
source: At stage 7, cells were much less active (Figure 4c, Video 6).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4c and Video 6 through live imaging.

claim: The pulsing amplitude is 40% of mean variation at stage 3 and only about 15% in the equatorial part at stage 7.
source: This difference was confirmed by monitoring the variation of the relative apical surface of individual cells (Figure 4e) or a whole population (Figure 4f) (40% of mean variation at stage 3 and only about 15% in the equatorial part at stage 7).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 4e and 4f.

claim: The pulsing amplitude gradually decreases in the mediolateral region from stage 3 to stage 8.
source: Quantification of the average variation of the apical cell surface in a series of follicles indicates that the pulsing amplitude gradually decreases in the mediolateral region from stage 3 to stage 8 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: At the poles of stage 3-4 and stage 7-8 follicles, the pulse activity is high.
source: We managed to image the poles of stage 3–4 and stage 7–8 follicles, and in both cases the pulse activity is high (Figure 4b,d–f, Videos 7 and 8).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4b,d–f, Videos 7 and 8 through live imaging of poles.

claim: Analysis of slightly tilted stage 7-8 follicles reveals a gradient of pulse intensity emanating from the pole.
source: Finally, the analysis of slightly tilted stage 7–8 follicles clearly revealed a gradient of pulse intensity emanating from the pole (Figure 4g and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4g and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The pulse intensity distribution is similar in space and time to the JAK-STAT activity gradient.
source: Thus, the pulse intensity distribution is similar in space and time to the JAK-STAT activity gradient.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of pulse intensity gradient and JAK-STAT gradient patterns.

claim: The cell pulse amplitude is significantly reduced in the mediolateral region of stage 3-4 follicles and near the poles of stage 7-8 upd RNAi follicles.
source: Moreover, the cell pulse amplitude is significantly reduced in the mediolateral region of stage 3–4 follicles and near the poles of stage 7–8 upd RNAi follicles (Figure 4h,i, Videos 9 and 10), indicating that JAK-STAT regulates FC apical pulsatory activity.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4h,i, Videos 9 and 10.

claim: JAK-STAT regulates FC apical pulsatory activity.
source: Moreover, the cell pulse amplitude is significantly reduced in the mediolateral region of stage 3–4 follicles and near the poles of stage 7–8 upd RNAi follicles (Figure 4h,i, Videos 9 and 10), indicating that JAK-STAT regulates FC apical pulsatory activity.
evidence: Inferred from upd RNAi experiments showing reduced pulse amplitude.

claim: Clonal ectopic activation of JAK is sufficient to increase pulse intensity in the mediolateral region of stage 7-8 follicles when compared to similar control clones.
source: Finally, we found that clonal ectopic activation of JAK is sufficient to increase pulse intensity in the mediolateral region of stage 7–8 follicles when compared to similar control clones (Figure 4j, Videos 11 and 12).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4j, Videos 11 and 12.

claim: The JAK-STAT pathway has an instructive role in controlling the intensity of FC apical pulses, leading to a specific spatiotemporal pattern breaking follicle symmetry in each hemisphere.
source: Together, these results show that the JAK-STAT pathway has an instructive role in controlling the intensity of FC apical pulses, leading to a specific spatiotemporal pattern breaking follicle symmetry in each hemisphere.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments.

claim: The apical level of the Myosin II active form is significantly reduced by 18% in STAT92E null mutant clones on young follicles when compared to WT surrounding cells.
source: The apical level of the Myosin II active form, visualized by its phosphorylation, is significantly reduced by 18% in STAT92E null mutant clones on young follicles when compared to WT surrounding cells (n = 17 clones, p<0,001), which may suggest that MyoII activity is regulated by JAK-STAT signaling (Figure 5a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5a with n=17 clones, p<0.001.

claim: Clonal gain of function of JAK in the mediolateral region at stage 7-8 does not increase the apical phosphorylation level of MyoII.
source: However, clonal gain of function of JAK in the region where the JAK-STAT pathway is normally inactive (mediolateral at stage 7–8) does not increase the apical phosphorylation level of MyoII (Figure 5b).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Analysis of the global pattern of apical MyoII phosphorylation does not reveal any gradient between the poles and the mediolateral regions.
source: Moreover, analysis of the global pattern of apical MyoII phosphorylation does not reveal any gradient between the poles and the mediolateral regions (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: MyoII activation by phosphorylation is independent of JAK-STAT signaling.
source: Altogether,these data indicate that MyoII activation by phosphorylation is independent of JAK-STAT signaling and that JAK-STAT regulates pulses by another means, which might be required for efficient apical recruitment of MyoII.
evidence: Inferred from lack of MyoII phosphorylation gradient and lack of increase with JAK gain-of-function.

claim: JAK-STAT and Myosin II control pulses in parallel.
source: Thus, although JAK-STAT and Myosin II are both required for early elongation, they control pulses in parallel.
evidence: Inferred from independent effects on pulses and lack of direct regulation of MyoII by JAK-STAT.

claim: Analysis of the eAR of the poles containing sqh mutant clones indicates that Myosin II loss of function specifically affects the elongation of the anterior pole, compared to the opposite WT posterior poles.
source: Analysis of the eAR of the poles containing such mutant clones indicates that Myosin II loss of function specifically affects the elongation of this pole, compared to the opposite WT posterior poles (n = 10) (Figure 5f,i).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5f,i with n=10.

claim: Clones in the mediolateral regions never induce elongation defects.
source: Moreover, we never observed clones in the mediolateral regions inducing elongation defects (n = 35) (Figure 5h).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5h with n=35.

claim: Rok null mutant clones affect elongation when situated at the pole.
source: Finally, we also performed similar experiment with Rok null mutant clones. Such clones have a weaker effect on cell morphology (Figure 5j and Wang and Riechmann, 2007), but still affect elongation when situated at the pole (Figure 5f,j).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5f,j, with citation to Wang and Riechmann, 2007.

claim: MyoII and Rok are required specifically at the poles to induce early elongation.
source: Thus, MyoII and Rok are required specifically at the poles to induce early elongation.
evidence: Inferred from clonal analysis showing effects only at poles.

claim: The gradient of apical isotropic FC pulses is the force-generating mechanism that drives early elongation.
source: These results strongly argue that the gradient of apical isotropic FC pulses is the force-generating mechanism that drives early elongation.
evidence: Inferred from requirement of MyoII at poles and correlation with pulse gradient.

claim: Cells are slightly elongated perpendicularly to the axis of elongation and this morphology did not change significantly over time.
source: However, cells are actually slightly elongated perpendicularly to the axis of elongation and this morphology did not change significantly over time, indicating that this parameter does not contribute to follicle elongation during early stages (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: The orientation of cytokinesis figures did not highlight any bias towards the AP axis.
source: We therefore quantified the orientation of cytokinesis figures, which did not highlight any bias towards the AP axis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The number of cells in the longest line of the AP axis significantly increases between stage 6 and 8.
source: As follicle cells from stage 6 onwards stop dividing and their number remains constant, we counted the number of cells in the longest line of the AP axis (i.e., the follicle plane that includes the polar cells). This number significantly increases between stage 6 and 8, showing that cells intercalate in this line (Figure 6a–d).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6a–d through cell counting.

claim: The number of cells in the longest line of the AP axis is correlated with the follicle AR.
source: This number is also correlated with the follicle AR (Figure 6e), indicating that follicle early elongation is associated with cell intercalation along the AP axis.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Follicle early elongation is associated with cell intercalation along the AP axis.
source: This number is also correlated with the follicle AR (Figure 6e), indicating that follicle early elongation is associated with cell intercalation along the AP axis.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between cell number in AP axis and aspect ratio.

claim: The cell apical surface is lower at the poles than in more equatorial cells, and this difference increases during the early elongation phase.
source: We observed that the cell apical surface is lower at the poles than in more equatorial cells, and that this difference increases during the early elongation phase (Figure 6f,g,h).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6f,g,h.

claim: Cell height is significantly larger at the poles.
source: Cell height is significantly larger at the poles, indicating that the changes in apical surface are linked to cell morphology, as previously shown during mesoderm invagination for instance (Figure 6i) (He et al., 2014).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6i, with citation to He et al., 2014.

claim: Cells at the poles have a lower volume than those in the mediolateral region at stage 7.
source: However, cells at the poles have a lower volume than those in the mediolateral region at stage 7 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The difference of volume is proportionally weaker than the change in apical surface, suggesting the cell shape changes induce the reduction of volume rather than the opposite.
source: This difference of volume is nonetheless proportionally weaker than the change in apical surface, suggesting the cell shape changes induce the reduction of volume rather than the opposite.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of volume and apical surface changes.

claim: Early elongation is associated with a moderate cell constriction in the polar regions.
source: Thus, early elongation is associated with a moderate cell constriction in the polar regions.
evidence: Inferred from reduced apical surface and increased height at poles.

claim: FCs that are mutant for Stat92E are flattened, with a larger surface and a lower height, compared to WT surrounding cells.
source: Interestingly, FCs that are mutant for Stat92E are also flattened, with a larger surface and a lower height, compared to WT surrounding cells (Figure 6j–m).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6j–m.

claim: The apical cell surface at the poles of stages 7-8 is increased by the loss of function of Upd.
source: Moreover, the apical cell surface at the poles of stages 7–8 is increased by the loss of function of Upd (Figure 6h).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6h.

claim: Early elongation is associated with apical cell constriction at the poles and with oriented cell rearrangements.
source: Early elongation is associated with apical constriction at the poles and with oriented cell rearrangements, but without any visible planar cell polarization of the apical domain.
evidence: Summary statement from Abstract based on multiple observations.

claim: Follicle elongation can be subdivided into at least two main temporal and mechanistic phases: an early one (stages 3-6) that is independent of Fat2, rotation, and ECM and F-actin basal polarization, and a second one (stages 7-14) that requires Fat2.
source: The first main conclusion of this work is that follicle elongation can be subdivided into at least two main temporal and mechanistic phases: an early one (stages 3–6) that is independent of Fat2, rotation, and ECM and F-actin basal polarization, and a second one (stages 7–14) that requires Fat2.
evidence: Summary conclusion from Discussion based on fat2 mutant analysis.

claim: Fat2 is required as early as the germarium for the correct planar polarization of the microtubule cytoskeleton and for follicle rotation.
source: Nevertheless, Fat2 is required as early as the germarium for the correct planar polarization of the microtubule cytoskeleton and for follicle rotation, which takes place during the early elongation phase (Viktorinová and Dahmann, 2013; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Viktorinová and Dahmann, 2013; Chen et al., 2016.

claim: The rotation reinforces the basal pcp of the F-actin during stages 4-6.
source: The rotation reinforces the basal pcp of the F-actin during stages 4–6, and thus probably participates in the late phase in this way (Cetera et al., 2014; Aurich and Dahmann, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cetera et al., 2014; Aurich and Dahmann, 2016.

claim: Rotation is necessary for the deposition of ECM fibrils.
source: Rotation is also necessary for the deposition of ECM fibrils, although their specific role in elongation has not been clearly elucidated yet.
evidence: Statement about rotation and ECM fibrils with acknowledgment of uncertainty.

claim: The ECM stiffness gradient contribution begins only at stage 7-8.
source: Another mechanism that participates in elongation is the ECM stiffness gradient (Crest et al., 2017). However, its contribution begins only at stage 7–8.
evidence: Supported by citation to Crest et al., 2017.

claim: vkg (ColIV) loss-of-function follicles elongate correctly up to stage 8, showing that the ECM is required only in the second elongation phase.
source: This is in agreement with the fact that the ECM stiffness gradient depends on Fat2 and that vkg (ColIV) loss-of-function follicles elongate correctly up to stage 8, showing that the ECM is required only in the second elongation phase (Crest et al., 2017; Haigo and Bilder, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crest et al., 2017; Haigo and Bilder, 2011.

claim: The early elongation phase requires elements of the apical side of follicle cells, whereas the second phase involves the basal side.
source: Notably, the early elongation phase requires elements of the apical side of follicle cells, whereas the second phase involves the basal side.
evidence: Summary statement based on observations throughout the study.

claim: The fly germband extension involves both the apical and basal domain of cells.
source: Mirroring our observations, a recent report nicely shows that the fly germband extension, which was thought to depend exclusively on the apical domain of the cells, also involves their basal domain (Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2017.

claim: Both the gradients of apical pulses and of BM stiffness are under the control of JAK-STAT.
source: Moreover, both the gradients of apical pulses and of BM stiffness are under the control of JAK-STAT, indicating that this pathway has a pleiotropic effect on follicle elongation.
evidence: Inferred from observations in this study and previous work on BM stiffness.

claim: Integrin and Pak contribute to early elongation in an indirect manner through their impact on the positioning, the differentiation or the survival of the polar cells.
source: We have also shown that integrin and Pak contribute to early elongation in an indirect manner through their impact on the positioning, the differentiation or the survival of the polar cells.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on genetic analysis of pak and mys mutants.

claim: Pak mutants have an altered germarium structure leading to abnormal follicle budding, suggesting that polar cell mispositioning might be linked to this primary defect.
source: Interestingly, Pak mutants also have an altered germarium structure leading to abnormal follicle budding, suggesting that polar cell mispositioning might be linked to this primary defect (Vlachos et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vlachos et al., 2015.

claim: Pak might be required for early elongation in a more direct manner than polar cell positioning, downstream of or in parallel to the JAK-STAT pathway, but independently of basal planar polarization.
source: However, it is worth noticing that Pak mutant follicles do not elongate at all, whereas they still have a cluster of polar cells. Thus, Pak might also be required for early elongation in a more direct manner than polar cell positioning, downstream of or in parallel to the JAK-STAT pathway, but independently of basal planar polarization.
evidence: Speculative inference based on Pak mutant phenotype.

claim: Polar cells define the elongation axis of each follicle during early elongation by secreting the Upd morphogen and by forming a gradient from each pole, which in turn induces apical pulses.
source: We found that polar cells define the elongation axis of each follicle during early elongation by secreting the Upd morphogen and by forming a gradient from each pole, which in turn induces apical pulses.
evidence: Summary conclusion from Discussion based on JAK-STAT experiments.

claim: JAK-STAT has been implicated in the elongation of different tissues in flies and in vertebrates.
source: JAK-STAT has already been implicated in the elongation of different tissues in flies and in vertebrates.
evidence: General statement about JAK-STAT function in development.

claim: Upd works as the elongation cue for the hindgut during fly embryogenesis, a process also associated with cell intercalation.
source: For instance, Upd works as the elongation cue for the hindgut during fly embryogenesis, a process also associated with cell intercalation, although the underlying mechanism is unknown (Johansen et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Johansen et al., 2003.

claim: JAK-STAT is involved in the extension-convergence mechanism during zebrafish gastrulation.
source: Maybe more significantly, JAK-STAT is involved in the extension-convergence mechanism during zebrafish gastrulation (Yamashita et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yamashita et al., 2002.

claim: JAK-STAT participates in tissue folding in the fly gut and wing disc.
source: Moreover, JAK-STAT also participates in other morphogenetic events, such as tissue folding in the fly gut and wing disc (Wells et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wells et al., 2013.

claim: Early elongation is associated with apical cell constriction close to the poles and oriented cell intercalations.
source: Nonetheless, we determined that early elongation is associated with apical cell constriction close to the poles and oriented cell intercalations.
evidence: Summary conclusion from cellular behavior analysis.

claim: Cell constriction is probably a direct consequence of apical pulses.
source: Cell constriction is probably a direct consequence of apical pulses, as has been shown in many other contexts, because both myosin II and JAK-STAT loss of function affect pulse and induce an increase of the apical surface (Wang and Riechmann, 2007; Martin and Goldstein, 2014).
evidence: Inferred from loss-of-function experiments, with citations to Wang and Riechmann, 2007; Martin and Goldstein, 2014.

claim: Cell constriction may accentuate the curvature at the poles and thus promote elongation.
source: Thus, as during tissue invagination, cell constriction may accentuate the curvature at the poles and thus promote elongation.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on analogy to tissue invagination.

claim: Intercalation can be induced at a tissue scale by long-range anisotropic tensions in the tissue.
source: Intercalation can be induced at a tissue scale by long-range anisotropic tensions in the tissue, as exemplified by the development of pupal wings or mammalian limb bud ectoderm (Aigouy et al., 2010; Lau et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aigouy et al., 2010; Lau et al., 2015.

claim: The apical pulses could act via the constriction, acting as a pulling force at each pole.
source: Here, the apical pulses could act in a similar way via the constriction, acting as a pulling force at each pole.
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed by analogy to wing development.

claim: Intercalations may correspond to a passive response, bringing plasticity to the tissue and hence stabilizing its elongation.
source: Thus, intercalations may correspond to a passive response, bringing plasticity to the tissue and hence stabilizing its elongation.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of intercalation role.

claim: A gradient of randomly oriented cell migration contributes to vertebrate AP axis elongation and is independent of pcp.
source: A gradient of randomly oriented cell migration contributes to vertebrate AP axis elongation and is, to our knowledge, the only other example of a tissue elongation mechanism instructed by a signaling cue and independent of pcp (Bénazéraf et al., 2010), in contrast to the many examples where pcp controls cell-movements that induce axis elongation in vertebrates.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bénazéraf et al., 2010.

claim: A morphogen gradient can trigger tissue elongation through a control of cell pulsing and without a planar cell polarity requirement.
source: Thus, a morphogen gradient can trigger tissue elongation through a control of cell pulsing and without a planar cell polarity requirement.
evidence: Summary conclusion from Abstract based on all findings.

claim: This simple mechanism may apply to other tissues and other morphogens.
source: This simple mechanism may apply to other tissues and other morphogens.
evidence: Speculative generalization of findings.
